studies.title: Yours And Mine
studies.meaning: The surah is a refusal, delivered as an order to say it. Four denials follow, arranged in two matched pairs. The repetition has occupied scholars for centuries. The most common readings separate present from future, or the act of worship from its object, and the sources record several without settling. The last line does not concede anything. It separates. You have your way and I have mine, said without heat.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The sources report the occasion consistently. Leading Meccans proposed a deal in which each side would worship the other's object for a year, so the dispute could be closed. The surah answers that proposal and shuts the door. It belongs to the period when opposition had turned into bargaining, which is usually a sign of pressure on both sides.

keyTerms.note: An imperative opening the surah, so the whole chapter is a quotation the reader is instructed to repeat. It puts the refusal into the mouth of anyone reciting it, not only the one first addressed.
The word covers a religion, a debt, and a judgement, all built on the sense of what is owed and to whom. Saying you have yours draws a line without conceding that both are equal.
A participle rather than a verb, so the third denial describes what a person is rather than what he does. Classical grammarians use exactly that difference to explain why the surah repeats itself.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Mecca ran on accommodation. The sanctuary held many gods and the town made its living from all of them, so a proposal to take turns was, by local standards, generous and obvious. Refusing it cost the community its last route to a quiet life. The surah is short and its tone is level, which is what makes the refusal final rather than a stage in a negotiation.
studies.didYouKnow: The early collections report that this surah and the one about God being one were recited together in certain prayers, morning and evening, as a pair. Read side by side they do opposite work. This one clears the ground of what is not God. The other states what he is.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The surah separates two things that are easily confused: tolerance and agreement. Nothing here attacks anyone, and no one is threatened. The ayat simply refuse to blend two objects of worship into one arrangement. That leaves a clear position and a peaceful one at the same time. Early scholars note that the last line states a fact rather than granting permission, which is why it can be said without anger.

crossReferences.why: States the same separation from the other direction, ruling out force in the matter this surah refuses to blend.
Answers the same kind of proposal with a question, in the voice of the one being asked.
Supplies the positive content this surah leaves out, and the two were recited together as a pair.

studies.applyIt: Think of one place where you have been softening a position to keep a relationship comfortable. Try saying the plain version of it once, to yourself, in the tone this surah uses. Level, unhurried, not an argument. Notice that being clear and being hostile are not the same thing. That is the whole technique of these six lines.
studies.explainEasier: God tells his messenger to say it plainly to those who reject him. I do not worship what you worship. You do not worship what I worship. You have your way, and I have mine.
